claims.text: The baseline catalyst is a nanoscale, equimolar, solid-solution PtPdRhRuIrOs alloy.
Ru is a lower-electronegativity metal relative to the higher-electronegativity metals it is proposed to replace.
Increasing the fraction of a lower-electronegativity metal such as Ru will enhance inter-site charge transfer in PtPdRhRuIrOs.
Electronegativity differences among elements in a high-entropy alloy can cause inter-site charge redistribution.
A Ru-enriched PtPdRhRuIrOs variant can retain the high-entropy solid-solution structure.
Changing alloy composition alters the catalyst's electronic structure.
Enhanced charge transfer in Ru-enriched PtPdRhRuIrOs will modify the adsorption energies of partially oxidized ethanol intermediates.
Optimizing intermediate adsorption energies will lower kinetic barriers for ethanol oxidation.
Lower kinetic barriers produced by optimized adsorption will improve overall ethanol-oxidation activity.
The Ru-enriched catalyst will have a lower ethanol-oxidation onset potential than the equimolar catalyst.
The Ru-enriched catalyst will have a higher ethanol-oxidation current density than the equimolar catalyst.
The predicted improvement depends on retaining a high-entropy solid-solution phase.
The predicted improvement is limited to moderate temperatures and a particular applied-potential range typical of ethanol oxidation.
Particle size, morphology, synthesis conditions, and electrochemical conditions should be held constant when comparing the equimolar and Ru-enriched catalysts.
In situ spectroscopic shifts in binding energy can be used as evidence of charge transfer and changed intermediate adsorption.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant onset-potential reduction and current-density increase, or failure to observe enhanced charge transfer and altered adsorption, would falsify the hypothesis.
The magnitude of the performance enhancement and the optimal Ru substitution level are experimentally undetermined.
